item.title: Dolly Parton's Imagination Library
item.description:
Source: imaginationlibrary.com

With today's news, I thought I'd share this great program:

“When I was growing up in the hills of East Tennessee, I knew my dreams would come true. I know there are children in your community with their own dreams. They dream of becoming a doctor or an inventor or a minister. Who knows, maybe there is a little girl whose dream is to be a writer and singer.

The seeds of these dreams are often found in books and the seeds you help plant in your community can grow across the world.”

Top Comment:

My daughter receives books through this program and I was curious how it was sustained at a $2.5/book wholesale cost.

Interestingly, the coordinating body that selects books, facilitates distribution, and negotiates wholesale pricing is the Dolly Parton Imagination Library, but per-book funding is actually entirely through local charities and so on. This means that where charities are unable to act as partners, children will not receive books, but it also means that the program can operate by growing and shrinking as local support (including from state and local government grants) comes online and goes offline while keeping the overhead for local partners low.

Dolly Parton came up with the initial local structure for her region in Tennessee and David Dotson of Dollywood scaled the operation using this decentralized model. Very impressive structure that makes this sustainable.

Here’s the interview where he talks about it: https://www.endbookdeserts.com/dolly-parton-imagination-libr...

I run a similar-in-spirit site about starting from scratch on a project and getting to something functional. I tried both ads and courses, in my case neither were very successful. I don't know if that's workable in the UI/UX world.

I've done only a small amount of web-design work over the years, but I can imagine that, if I landed on CSS-tricks trying to work out a tricky (to me) CSS or usability problem where LLMs had been failing me, and I had a quick and easy option to pay a few hundred dollars and meet with the guy who wrote the book, I might do that. That's also how I got a lot of my first customers in my current business; I offered paid phone calls where a user could pay a nominal rate and ask some upfront questions about a project they were working on. Many of those calls turned in to longer contracts, and the fee kept out the folks who were just looking to sell me something.

A lot of my customers have been organizations whose focus is not my industry, but, for one reason or another, they needed something done that fits in my wheelhouse. This means they don't (yet) want to hire this expertise and build processes internally, so they're willing to pay my premium rates. Perhaps there is a way to target these types of companies with custom services in the space.

Another commenter mentioned[0] that often ergonomic keyboards aren't columnar, but staggered. What if for the pin layout, instead of this:

    1  1  0  0
It was this?

    1  0  1  0
Then the keys could connect with at least two wires in either columnar or 50% stagger, using the same pins. Each key has a maximum of six neighbors instead of four, but that shouldn't be too much trouble.

Naturally if you expand to 6 pins it could support 0/33/66% stagger positions.

More cool, I think, is that it doesn't have to be aligned? You could imagine shifting the pins and mechanism over from top to bottom, so it's a 20%/70% stagger. Maybe that would make it structurally stronger, like how bricks are overlapped?

Very inspiring project, thanks for sharing.

item.title: Blaise Pascal invented fixed route public transport (2024)
item.description:
Source: humantransit.org

Top Comment:

The Carosses à cinq sols was not just an idea but a startup proper; Pascal invested most of what he owned for a sixth of the business, which turned out to be a great investment.

The main idea behind it was a kind of time share. At the time, only the (very) rich could afford to own and maintain carosses and stables with 6 to 10 horses in crowded cities like Paris; it was a truly revolutionary idea that a company would own the cars and the horses, and the general public would pay only for the time traveled.

Then the other genius idea, of course, was fixed routes and predictable schedule, as explained in the post. People actually objected at first that it would be stupid (and ruinous) to have empty carriages going from one place to another instead of chasing customers like a modern cab. But that was the whole point.

item.description:

Why do people try to vibecode PDF engines that already exist in Rust? https://github.com/yfedoseev/pdf_oxide which this project builds on completely misses https://github.com/fschutt/printpdf which was already developed with tons of fixes over years (both with and without AI). MIT license and also builds on WASM with a demo running on https://fschutt.github.io/printpdf/

One Google search (yeah I'm old, sorry, nobody "Googles" anymore) for "rust pdf library" shows this. Yet people now redo and redo and redo everything again just to have "their" semi-broken copy of a HTML -> PDF renderer (and then run into the same edge cases that were already fixed before). There are lots of edge cases in typography especially, I recently had a lot of fixes as I was trying to ocr-and-cleanup a 1732 scan of some books with Claude auto-extracting the font. There were a ton of edge cases in the layout, esp. related to column, footnote and sidebar handling, or things like "Hebrew RTL text accidentally disappears if text breaks weirdly", "1-bit image compression", etc.

I have nothing against AI, I use it heavily myself, but what is annoying is people completely ignoring the years of work of existing projects that do the exact same thing - instead of just forking, but instead re-tokenizing the exact same work again. Most likely the author didn't research "does this already exist" and that's annoying, then you get 100 of similar projects reinventing the world with tokens again and again. Sometimes its beneficial and can lead to faster exploration of new approaches, but in most cases its not and misses edge cases that were solved before.
